title: Normalize provisioning handlers and optimize capacity allocator
creator: Aisha Verma
description: Background: Over time several separate provisioning handlers and legacy scheduler code paths accumulated in the GPU fleet controller and capacity planner. This has produced inconsistent node state transitions, occasional double-allocation of theoretical capacity, and complex retry logic that makes behavioral reasoning and testing difficult. Problem statement: We are seeing sporadic spikes in overprovisioning (nodes held idle while new nodes are created) and a handful of incidents where node lease state drifted between PROVISIONING -> PENDING_DELETE -> ACTIVE, causing jobs to be scheduled on node that was about to be torn down. Goal: Consolidate provisioning handlers into a single normalized event handler, remove duplicate capacity bookkeeping, and optimize the allocator algorithms to reduce overprovisioning and reduce slow path allocations. Expected impact: 15-25% reduction in excess reserved GPUs for common workload traces, 20% faster path from allocation request to RUNNING node in median case, and simpler lifecycle reasoning for future feature work.
acceptance_criteria: All provisioning logic for GPU nodes is routed through the new /provisioning/handler with a single canonical state machine
Capacity planner produces a consistent capacity estimate with no duplicate counting in 100% of unit tests and synthetic traces
End-to-end integration test shows median allocation latency reduced by >=15% and p95 not regressing
No functional regressions for Dedicated and Private deployment modes (same API behavior and SLOs)
Migration plan applied: legacy scheduler code flagged as deprecated and toggled off behind runtime feature flag
implementation_notes: Introduce new event envelope: ProvisionEvent{request_id, desired_capacity_delta, lease_id, origin} and deprecate ProvisionalLease and LeaseShadow handlers
Add canonical state transitions: NEW -> RESERVED -> PROVISIONING -> ACTIVE -> DRAINING -> TERMINATING
Centralize capacity accounting in capacity-allocator service (remove ad-hoc counters in fleet-controller)
Remove the historical ‘soft-reserve’ path; replace with time-boxed speculative allocation that can be reclaimed deterministically
Refactor the autoscaler queue to publish idempotent allocation intents instead of raw node commands
Keep legacy handlers behind feature flag: fleet.allocator.normalize_provisioning (default off for first two weeks of rollout)
migration_plan: Week 1: Unit tests + integration harness verifying state machine coverage for existing traces
Week 2: Canary deploy new allocator on a single shard (region-us-west2) with feature flag off; run A/B load replay and compare metrics
Week 3: Enable feature flag for 10% of traffic; monitor overprovisioning and allocation latency dashboards
Week 4: Ramp to 50% and then 100% if no regression; switch off legacy handlers and remove dead code in a follow-up cleanup PR
Rollout rollback criteria: >5% increase in p95 allocation latency or >10% increase in reserved GPU count sustained over 30m
test_plan: Unit tests for canonical state transitions and idempotency (new test suite: allocator_state_test.go)
Synthetic trace replay using historical booking traces v2025-Q4 to validate capacity numbers
Integration: end-to-end allocation test from request -> node RUNNING with simulated cloud provider (mock-driver)
Chaos: simulate node preemption and lease reconciliation while allocator is enabled
Performance: bench capacity algorithm with 10k concurrent allocation intents and measure median/p95 latency
rollout_plan: Create feature-flag gate and canary pipeline: deploy to staging, then region-us-west2 shard
Run daily smoke checks and automated SLO verification for first 72 hours
If stable, update Dedicated docs to reflect no behavior change but note improved provisioning latency
Schedule follow-up cleanup ticket to remove flag and legacy handlers after 4 weeks of stable operation
